questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y).
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x+y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡z.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡z.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={tan}^{2}⁡(3x-5y).
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=3x-5y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=3x-5y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3-5\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={tan}^{2}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3-5{tan}^{2}⁡z.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=3-5{tan}^{2}⁡z.$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{z}^{3}}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=\frac{1}{{z}^{3}}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{{e}^{y-x}}{x-y+1}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-\frac{{e}^{-z}}{z+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{e}^{-z}}{z+1}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(z+1){e}^{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int (z+1){e}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z+1 & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{z} & \,⟹\,v={e}^{z}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (z+1){e}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ (z+1){e}^{z}-\int {e}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ (z+1){e}^{z}-{e}^{z} & =x+C \\ z{e}^{z} & =x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
(x-y){e}^{x-y}=x+C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=(x-y){e}^{x-y}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{e}^{x+y}-x-y}{x+y}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{{e}^{z}-z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{e}^{z}}{z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{z}{{e}^{z}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z{e}^{-z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-z} & \,⟹\,v=-{e}^{-z}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z{e}^{-z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -z{e}^{-z}+\int {e}^{-z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -z{e}^{-z}-{e}^{-z} & =x+C \\ -{e}^{-z}(z+1) & =x+K \\ {e}^{-z}(z+1) & =C-x\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
{e}^{-x-y}(x+y+1)=C-x
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={e}^{-x-y}(x+y+1).$

Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2y)}-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-2x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡z & =x+K \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡z & =C-2x,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y)=C-2x\,\,
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y).$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+2}-1.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=\frac{x+C}{x+y},
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int (\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2 & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{z} \\ {v}^{′}=1 & \,⟹\,v=z\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ z(\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)-\int \text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ z(\operatorname{ln}⁡z+2)-z & =x+C \\ z(\operatorname{ln}⁡z+1) & =x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1) & =x+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1 & =\frac{x+C}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Reducing a First-Order ODE to a Simpler Form Using a Linear Substitution
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \ln(x + y).
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z= x + y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form $z'(x) = f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z = x + y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 1 + \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} - 1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form $z'(x) = f(z),$ we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = \ln z+1.
$$

Therefore, $f(z) = \ln z + 1.$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Reducing a First-Order ODE to a Simpler Form Using a Linear Substitution

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving a First-Order ODE Using a Linear Substitution
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = x + y.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y) = x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z = x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 1 + \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} - 1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form $z'(x) = f(z)$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = z+1.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{z+1}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{z+1}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|z+1| & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\ln{|x+y+1|}  = x + C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y) = \ln{|x+y+1|}.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we have a differential equation of the form 

$$
y ' = f ( a x + b y ),
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are real constants. In this case, we can rewrite the equation as a separable differential equation using the substitution $z= ax+by.$ We then proceed to solve this separable equation.

 To see how we apply this method, let's consider the following example: 

$$
y' = (x+y)^2
$$

First, we make the substitution

$$
z = x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 1 + \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} - 1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form $z'(x) = g(z)$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = z^2+ 1.
$$

Notice that this differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{z}^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{arctan}⁡z & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the general solution to the equation in terms of $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\arctan {(x+y)}  = x + C
$$
